(p-177) Surah al-‘Alaq is Meccan, and its verses number nineteen.

﴿Read﴾ — that is, what is revealed to you, for the command to read necessarily requires something to be read; and since it is not specified, it must be that which is directly connected to the command. Whether or not this surah was the first to be revealed, the closest view is that this refers to His saying, ﴿what he did not know﴾, which was the first revelation to him (peace and blessings be upon him), as the well-known hadith of al-Zuhri indicates. His saying, ﴿in the name of your Lord﴾, is connected to an implied verb that is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to the subject pronoun, meaning: read while associated with His name, the Exalted — that is, beginning with it, so that its accompaniment to all parts of what is read is realized. The mention of the title "Lord," which signifies nurturing and conveying (tarbiyah and tabligh) step by step to the fitting perfection, together with its attribution to his pronoun (peace be upon him), indicates that he (peace be upon him) was conveyed by the revelation that is widely transmitted to the furthest limit of human perfections. The description of the Lord in His saying, ﴿who created﴾, serves to remind of the first of the bounties bestowed upon him (peace be upon him) from Him, the Exalted, and to alert that whoever is able to create man with the life he has and what follows it of scientific and practical perfections, from a substance that had not even smelled the fragrance of life, let alone other perfections, is able to teach reading to the living, knowing, speaking one. That is, the One who originated creation and is its sole possessor, or who created everything.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 96, verse 2:

﴿Created man﴾. On the first reading, the specification of the creation of man by mention, out of all other created beings, is because he is singled out for the wonders of craftsmanship and governance. On the second reading, it is a singling out of man from among all other created beings by the explanation (bayan) and an exaltation of his station, since he is the most noble of them, the Revelation was sent down to him, and he is the one commanded to recite. It is also permissible that the first verb be intended to mean the creation of man as well, and that its being stripped of an object is intended to convey generality (al-ibham), after which the explanation (al-tafsir) comes as a means of magnifying his natural disposition (fitrah). His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿from a clot﴾, that is: a congealed blood, to explain the perfection of His power, may He be exalted, by manifesting the clear contrast between his first state and his final state. Its being expressed in the plural form, on the basis that man is in the sense of the plural, is for the sake of observing the rhyme (fawasil). Perhaps this is the secret of singling it out by mention from among the other stages of the human natural disposition, even though the drop of semen and the dust are more indicative of the perfection of power, since they are further removed from humanity. Since the creation of man was the first of the blessings flowing from Him, may He be exalted, upon him, peace and blessings be upon him, and the most ancient of the proofs indicating His existence, may He be mighty and majestic, and the perfection of His power, knowledge and wisdom, He, may He be exalted, described His essence with that first, so that he, peace be upon him, might cite it as evidence for His enabling him to recite, then He repeated the command with His saying, may He be exalted:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 96, verse 3:

﴿Read﴾. That is: do what you have been commanded, as an emphasis on the obligation and a preparation for what follows it, namely the words of the Exalted: ﴿And your Lord is the Most Generous﴾... and so on. For it is a new, independent statement, coming to remove the excuse that he (peace be upon him) had stated in his words (peace be upon him): ﴿I am not a reciter﴾. He means that reading is the business of one who writes and reads, whereas I am unlettered (ummi). So it was said to him: Your Lord, who commanded you to read, beginning with His name, is the Most Generous.
Who taught by the pen. That is: He taught what He taught through the medium of the pen and not otherwise. Just as He taught the reader through writing and the pen, He teaches you without them.

The Most High's words: ﴿He taught man that which he knew not﴾ are a substitutive apposition (badal al-ishtimal) of "taught by the pen", meaning: He taught him by it and without it, of the matters both universal and particular, both manifest and hidden, that had not occurred to his mind. The omission of the object at first, and its mention afterward under the heading of "not being known", indicates the perfection of His power and the perfection of His generosity, and it signals that He teaches him knowledge that the intellects cannot encompass, which is not hidden.

"Kallā" is a rebuke to the one who disbelieves in the blessing of Allah, the Exalted, through his transgression, even though no mention of him has preceded it, for the sake of intensifying the admonition. And His saying, the Exalted, ﴿Indeed, mankind does transgress﴾ means: he surely exceeds the limit and is arrogant toward his Lord. It is an explanation of the one being rebuked and of that from which he is rebuked. It has been said: this, up to the end of the surah, was revealed concerning Abu Jahl after a period of time, and this is the apparent view.

The Almighty's words, ﴿that he sees himself as self-sufficient﴾, are an object of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*, the object showing reason). The meaning is: he transgresses because he sees himself as self-sufficient. It is also said that "istaghna" (اسْتَغْنى) is a second object of "ra'a" (رَأى), since here it means "knew" (عَلِمَ). This is why its subject and object can be two pronouns referring to the same person, as in "*'alimtunī*" (عَلِمْتُنِي, "you knew me"). Some have permitted this even for the visual sense of "ra'a," and they cite as an example the words of Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her: "We were with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and we had no food except the two black ones." The reason for his transgression is attributed to his seeing himself, not to self-sufficiency itself, as the Almighty's words indicate: ﴿And if Allah had expanded provision for His servants, they would have committed excess on earth﴾. This is to make clear that the basis of his transgression is his corrupt belief.

It is narrated that Abu Jahl said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Do you claim that whoever is self-sufficient transgresses? Then make the mountains of Mecca silver and gold for us, so that we may take from them and transgress, and abandon our religion and follow yours." Then Jibril, peace be upon him, descended upon him and said: "If you wish, We shall do that; then if they do not believe, We shall do to them what We did to the people of the table (al-Ma'idah)." So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) refrained from supplicating, out of concern for them.

Abu al-Su'ud's commentary (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim), on surah 96, verse 8:

(p-179) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, to your Lord is the return﴾ is a threat to the tyrant and a warning to him of the consequence of tyranny. The shift (al-iltifat, a sudden change of grammatical person) serves to intensify the threat. "Al-Ruj'a" (the return) is a verbal noun meaning "the returning," like "al-Bushra" (the good news). The fronting of the prepositional phrase ("ila rabbika," to your Lord) before the predicate serves to restrict the return to Him, meaning: indeed, to the Owner of your affair is the return of all, by death and resurrection, not to anyone else, neither independently nor in partnership. So then you will see the consequence of your tyranny.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 96, verses 9–10:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Have you seen the one who forbids﴾ ﴿a servant when he prays?﴾ is a condemnation and a denunciation of his condition, and an expression of astonishment at it, and a notification that it is of such heinousness and strangeness that everyone to whom sight is possible ought to see it and be struck with wonder at it. It is narrated that Abu Jahl said among a group of the tyrants of Quraysh: "If I see Muhammad praying, I will surely trample his neck." Then he saw him (ﷺ) in prayer, so he went towards him, then turned back on his heels. They said: "What is the matter with you?" He said: "Between me and him there is a trench of fire, and terror, and wings." So this was revealed. The word "servant" (ʿabd) and its indefiniteness (being unspecified) serve to magnify him (ﷺ), to emphasise the enormity of the prohibition, and to reinforce the astonishment at it. The seeing here is visual (baṣariyyah).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 96, verses 9–10:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Have you seen the one who forbids﴾ ﴿a servant when he prays?﴾ is a condemnation and a denunciation of his condition, and an expression of astonishment at it, and a notification that it is of such heinousness and strangeness that everyone to whom sight is possible ought to see it and be struck with wonder at it. Regarding what is in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Have you seen if he was upon guidance﴾ ﴿or enjoined righteousness?﴾
Regarding what is in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Have you seen if he was upon guidance﴾ ﴿or enjoined righteousness?﴾

Regarding His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Have you considered, if he denies and turns away?﴾, its meaning is interrogative in the sense of "inform me" (akhbirni). Since sight (al-ru'ya) was a means to giving information about the seen object, the question about it was treated as a question about its object (mutaʿallaq). The address is to everyone who is fit to be addressed. The command, the denial and the turning away are placed within the conditional (al-shart) structure, which is undecided between occurring and not occurring. This is not by considering the acts themselves insofar as they proceed from the doer, for that is not within the scope of uncertainty at all; rather it is by considering their attributes, which are being a command to piety, denial, and turning away, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: Have you considered, if it is from Allah and you have disbelieved in it?﴾, as has passed.

The first object of "ara'ayta" (a-ra'aita) is omitted, and it is a pronoun referring back to the relative (al-mawsul), or a demonstrative pointing to it. Its second object is filled by the conditional sentence with its omitted apodosis (jawab), for the second object of "ara'ayta" can only be an interrogative sentence or an oath sentence. The meaning is: inform me, that forbidder, if he is upon guidance in what he forbids of worshipping Allah, exalted is He, or a commander to piety in what he commands of worshipping idols as he believes, or one who denies the truth and turns away from the right course as we say.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 96, verse 14:

﴿Did he not know that Allah sees?﴾ That is: He observes his conditions and therefore recompenses him for them, until he became bold enough to do what he did. The reason why the denial and the turning away were stated separately, as an independent conditional clause coupled with its answer and introduced by a fresh interrogative, and were not strung together in the same series as the first condition by conjoining them to "kāna" (if he was), is to signal that each of them stands on its own in reality and entails the threat that the answer expresses. As for the first part, it is something impossible, and it was mentioned within the scope of the condition in order to widen the scope of the matter. This is the secret behind detaching the first conditional clause from its answer and referring it to the answer of the second. Furthermore, it has been said that the first "ara'ayta" (tell me) means "akhbirni" (inform me), whose first object is the relative pronoun, and whose second object is the first conditional clause with its omitted answer, because the answer of the second conditional clause indicates it. The "ara'ayta" in both places is a repetition for emphasis. Its meaning is: Tell me about the one who forbids a servant of Allah from his prayer, if that forbidder is on a sound path in what he forbids from worshipping Allah the Exalted, or if he is commanding righteousness and piety in what he commands regarding the worship of idols, as he believes; and likewise if he is in denial of the truth and turning away from the correct religion, as we say: ﴿Did he not know that Allah sees?﴾ and observes his conditions, whether of guidance or of misguidance, and recompenses him according to that. So reflect. It has also been said that the meaning is: Tell me about the one who forbids a worshipper who prays, while the one forbidden is commanding guidance and piety, and the forbidder is a denier who turns away; how strange is this. It has also been said that the second address is to the disbeliever, for He the Exalted is like a judge before whom two litigants have appeared, addressing this one at one time and the other at another time; as if He had said: O disbeliever, tell me, if his prayer is guidance and his call to Allah the Exalted is a command to piety, would you forbid him? It has been said: he is Umayyah ibn Khalaf, who used to forbid Salman from prayer.

﴿Kallā﴾ (No!) is a rebuke to the forbidding, accursed one and a humiliation for him. The lam in His words, ﴿la-in lam yantahi﴾ (Indeed, if he does not desist), is the lam that prepares for an oath (lam al-muwatti'a lil-qasam), meaning: By Allah, if he does not desist from what he is upon and does not refrain.

﴿la-nasfa'an bil-nasiyah﴾ (We will surely seize him by the forelock). That is: We will indeed take hold of his forelock and drag him by it into the Fire. Al-safa' is grasping a thing and pulling it with harshness and force. It is also read as "nasfa'anna" with a doubled nun, and as "la-as-fa'anna." Its writing in the Mushaf with an alif follows the rule of pausing (hukm al-waqf), and the lam of definiteness (lam al-'ahd) is used in place of the possessive addition, since it is evident that the intended meaning is the forelock of the one mentioned.

﴿A lying, sinning forelock﴾ is a *badal* (substitute, or apposition) for "النَّاصِيَةِ" (*al-nasiyah*, "the forelock"). Its substitution for a definite noun is permitted even though it is *nakira* (indefinite), because it is qualified by its description. It is also read in the nominative, as "هِيَ ناصِيَةٌ" (*hiya nasiyatun*, "it is a forelock"), and in the accusative. Both readings are for vilification and abuse. Describing the forelock as lying and sinning is a *isnad majazi* (metaphorical attribution), and these qualities actually belong to its owner. It has an eloquence that is absent from saying "ناصِيَةُ كاذِبٍ المُخْطئِ" (*nasiyatu kadhibin al-mukhti'*, "the forelock of a liar, the sinner").

﴿Then let him call upon his council﴾, that is, the people of his assembly, so that they may help him. The nadi is the gathering place where the people hold their meetings (yantadi), that is, they assemble. It is narrated that Abu Jahl passed by the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while he was praying, and said: "Did I not forbid you?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) spoke harshly to him, and he said: "Do you threaten me, when I am the one with the most council in the valley?!" Then this was revealed.

﴿We shall call the guardians of Hell﴾ to drag him into the Fire. The word az-Zabaniyah (the angels of punishment, lit. "those who push") has the singular zabniyah, on the pattern of ʿifriyah, from az-zabn, which means pushing away. It has also been said that the word is zabaniyy, as though it were derived from az-zabn and then altered, as in amsa (from amsi). Its original form is zabaniyy, and it is said that the zabaniyah are so called by replacing the yaʾ with a tāʾ. What is meant is the angels of punishment. (p-181) It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ): "If he were to call his assembly, the zabaniyah would seize him immediately."

[Kallā] is a rebuke upon a rebuke and a warning upon a warning.

﴿Do not obey him﴾, that is: persist in what you are upon of his disobedience. ﴿And prostrate yourself﴾ and be constant in your prostration and your prayer, paying him no heed. ﴿And draw near﴾, and come closer to your Lord by that.

In a hadith: "The closest a servant is to his Lord is when he is prostrating."

From the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surah al-'Alaq is given a reward as if he had recited the entire Mufassal."
